summary: Removes a restriction on the MPLS reserved labels IPv4 Explicit NULL and IPv6 Explicit NULL. They were previously legal only at the bottom of the label stack; this document allows them anywhere in the stack. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: In a stack of plates, a special plate could only go at the bottom. This memo says the special plate may now go anywhere in the stack.

subtitle: MPLS Explicit NULL labels may now sit anywhere in the label stack, not just at the bottom.

tldr.problem: RFC 3032 said the IPv4 and IPv6 Explicit NULL labels were legal only at the bottom of an MPLS label stack, but in practice it is useful to send packets with Explicit NULL higher up, and the rule made that hard to do interoperably.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4182 rewrites the two RFC 3032 paragraphs so that an Explicit NULL at the top of the stack simply means the stack is popped, and the packet is then handled by whatever label (or IP header) is exposed.
tldr.outcome: The restriction is gone, which lets the Differentiated Services Pipe Model work properly when an LSP tunnels other MPLS packets. This document updates RFC 3032 and is itself updated by RFC 5462 and RFC 7274.

facts.label: Old rule (RFC 3032)
facts.value: Legal only at the bottom of the stack

today: RFC 4182 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3032, and it has itself been updated by RFC 5462 and RFC 7274. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3032 defines two reserved label values, the IPv4 Explicit NULL and the IPv6 Explicit NULL. It also says they are legal only at the bottom of the MPLS label stack, but gives no reason for that restriction.

In practice there are situations where it is useful to send MPLS packets with Explicit NULL somewhere other than the bottom. The meaning of such a packet is obvious enough, yet RFC 3032 declares it illegal, which made these situations hard to handle in an interoperable way. RFC 4182 removes the restriction, so both labels are legal anywhere in the stack.
sections.eli5: An old rule said a special sticker could only go on the last page of a book, and nobody knew why. This memo tears up the rule because people kept needing the sticker on other pages.

sections.title: What the Change Says
sections.content:
RFC 3032 listed the reserved labels. Paragraph i defined value 0 as the IPv4 Explicit NULL and paragraph iii defined value 2 as the IPv6 Explicit NULL. Each said the label was only legal at the bottom of the stack and that the stack must be popped and the packet forwarded on its IPv4 or IPv6 header. RFC 4182 replaces both paragraphs.

Under the new wording, an Explicit NULL at the top of the stack means the stack must be popped. If it was not the only label, the label beneath it rises to the top, and the packet's disposition is based on that label. If it was the only label, the stack is now empty. The packet is then treated as an IPv4 packet (for label 0) or an IPv6 packet (for label 2), and its disposition is based on that IP header.
sections.eli5: When the special plate is on top, you lift it off. If another plate is underneath, you now look at that one. If there was only the special plate, you look at what was sitting on it, the actual food.

sections.title: The Problem with the Old Restriction
sections.content:
With the restriction in place, a router should not give a label distribution peer a binding of Explicit NULL to a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) unless Condition L holds: every MPLS packet the peer receives for that FEC carries only a single label stack entry. If Explicit NULL is bound anyway and Condition L fails, the peer is being asked to create illegal packets, and none of the MPLS specifications say what it should do then.

The RFC adds that Condition L rarely holds in practice and that in general it is not possible to tell whether it holds. Removing the restriction removes the question.
sections.eli5: It was like being told to hand out a special ticket only if every guest had exactly one coat. Nobody could check that, and nobody knew what to do when someone had two coats.

sections.title: The Pipe Model and Explicit NULL
sections.content:
The strongest reason for the change is the Pipe Model of RFC 3270, which describes MPLS support of Differentiated Services. In that model a tunneled packet carries two pieces of Diff-Serv information: the LSP Diff-Serv information, meaningful to nodes along the LSP up to and including the egress, and the tunneled Diff-Serv information, meaningful beyond the egress.

When the Pipe Model is used, it is common for the LSP egress to bind Explicit NULL to the tunnel's FEC. The LSP Diff-Serv information then travels in the EXP bits of the Explicit NULL entry, and the tunneled information travels below it, in the IP header DS bits or the EXP bits of the next label stack entry. If the LSP is tunneling MPLS packets, this puts Explicit NULL at the top of a stack that has other entries, which RFC 3032 made illegal.

Implementations handled the illegal packet differently. Some simply transmitted it. Others stripped the Explicit NULL, which discards the LSP Diff-Serv information and breaks the Pipe Model. The RFC notes an implementation might even drop the whole packet. An egress could use an ordinary label instead, but Explicit NULL lets it decide right away, without a Label Information Base lookup, that forwarding depends on whatever is below the label, which can help forwarding performance.
sections.eli5: Think of a parcel with a note for the delivery drivers on the outside label and a different note for the receiver inside. The special plate carries the drivers' note. Throwing it away to follow the old rule loses the note, so the rule had to go.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations that follow this specification interoperate correctly and correctly support the Pipe Model. Implementations that do not may fail to interoperate. In particular, if a router advertises a binding of Explicit NULL and its upstream LDP peer will not send packets with multiple label stack entries and Explicit NULL on top, then the Pipe Model cannot use Explicit NULL until that peer is brought into compliance.

A router built before this specification might discard any received packet that has multiple label stack entries and Explicit NULL as its top label. The RFC advises configuring any such router so that it does not advertise bindings to Explicit NULL.
sections.eli5: If one friend still follows the old rule, the new trick will not work with that friend until they learn it. Until then, do not offer them the special plate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document allows Explicit NULL to occur at any position in the label stack. The RFC states that this modification does not impose any new security considerations beyond those discussed in RFC 3032.
sections.eli5: Letting the special plate go anywhere in the stack does not open any new doors for trouble beyond the ones that were already there.
